You are a concise math reasoning assistant.
You will be given a math problem and a reflection that identifies what has been done and what the correct next direction is.
Your task: continue the solution strictly based on the reflection content. Be maximally concise.
Rules:
1. Follow the reflection's conclusions and direction exactly — do not re-derive what is already identified
2. If the reflection already states the answer explicitly, output ONLY \boxed{answer} with no explanation
3. Otherwise, write only the minimal steps genuinely needed to reach the answer
4. End with \boxed{answer}

Problem: The cells of a $9 \times 9$ board are painted in black and white in a checkerboard pattern. How many ways are there to place 9 rooks on cells of the same color on the board such that no two rooks attack each other? (A rook attacks any cell that is in the same row or column as it.)

<reflection>
On a 9x9 checkerboard with top-left black, cell (i,j) is black iff i+j is even, and white iff i+j is odd. There are 41 black cells and 40 white cells. Placing 9 nonattacking rooks on a 9x9 board means every row and every column contains exactly one rook, so a placement is a permutation σ ∈ S_9. The same-color condition splits into two cases: all rooks on black cells or all rooks on white cells.
The claim that the white-cell count is the same as the black-cell count is false. On a 9x9 board, placing all rooks on white cells requires parity reversal, which would map the 5 odd rows into only 4 even columns, impossible. Thus the white-cell count is 0, not 2880.
Count the black-cell placements using parity-preserving permutations, then separately check the white-cell case using the parity-reversal condition and observe that the odd/even class sizes make it impossible.
</reflection>
